activity.title: We built pFOG, a wearable device that helps Parkinson’s patients overcome freezing episodes, and won 1st place at the UC Berkeley AI Hackathon! Freezing of Gait (FOG) is a dangerous symptom of Parkinson’s where patients suddenly lose the ability to walk, often causing falls and serious injury. Recent research shows that mechanical stimulation to the leg can restore movement almost instantly. This weekend, at Cal Hacks my team ( Shuyu van Kerkwijk , Harry Cheng , and Isabel Lew) and I built a device to automate this treatment. Our 1D-CNN + LSTM model detects FOG in real time using IMU data. When a freezing episode is detected, a robotic wearable delivers a targeted "poke" to help the person resume walking. We also built a web interface for easy data collection, labeling, training, and inference so that anyone can personalize it to their unique gait. Medical robotics has the potential to empower millions to live fuller lives, and we hope pFOG is a small but meaningful poke in this direction. devpost: https://lnkd.in/gP68Kb5V research inspiration: https://lnkd.in/gdRNsANV

Did you know that 20,000 whales lose their lives to ship strikes every year? This tragedy is avoidable: in many cases, reducing ship speeds and rerouting to avoid high-risk areas comes at little to no cost to ship operators. At DeltaHacks , we built a solution in under 24 hours. WhaleBeing visualizes ship routes on top of a dynamically predicted whale distribution. To produce the distribution, we implemented a prediction model based on a research paper that uses satellite data of habitat suitability. We then developed our own algorithm to calculate route risk scores by analyzing whale distribution weights near route nodes, offering an actionable insight. We won 1st place overall out of 134 teams and also received the Dyson Innovation Award. Part of our winnings went toward whale conservation efforts, and we aim to scale WhaleBeing with better data/models and route suggestion feature. Ultimately, we hope to propose policy changes using WhaleBeing’s impact evaluation for companies. If you're interested in working with us, feel free to reach out! 🐋 Built with my amazing team Lucas Liao , Gordon Zhang , and Nathan Li. devpost for more details: https://lnkd.in/gmiGqmKn prediction model source: https://lnkd.in/grDk6YcA

Today, my sister came downstairs and thought my furry associate, Ginger, and I working together was a wholesome scene. But the picture she took captured more than just that. I never got to meet my mom's mom. She passed away from breast cancer. My mom has both first-degree and second-degree relatives who have battled or died from breast cancer. So you'd think getting coverage for hereditary cancer genetic testing would be straightforward. It wasn't. Today, I spent over four hours trying to push through an appeal for a denial my mom received after that testing. And while I'm glad Ginger felt relaxed, the chaos happening on the phone made me feel quite the opposite. I was bounced between the ordering practice, the testing center, a prior authorization management company, and the insurance company, each one pointing me somewhere else. My mom had been told an appeal letter was submitted. It wasn't. When I read through the denial, I realized the name of the test, the procedure codes, the medical necessity rationale, and the family history documentation had never been submitted properly. And as frustrating as that is, the more I learn about this system, the more I see it isn't always negligence. It's the result of a broken prior authorization and appeals workflow. Nothing is easy. Nothing is straightforward. Everything is costly. In the past month, Loryn Canty and I have spoken with medical assistants, administrators, and providers who are completely burnt out from fighting denials and appeals. That burden doesn't stop with insurers or front offices. Eventually it reaches the patient. Today, that patient was my mom. She’s a hardworking elementary school teacher and a single mom who has spent every second outside of work supporting my sister and me. She got this testing to understand her own inherited cancer risk, and what it could mean for her daughters. She shouldn't have to spend hours fighting for coverage she already pays for. No patient should. Sitting there, dialing number after number, fighting through robots on the phone, piecing together a denial that should have been handled months ago, I remembered exactly why I started building Praxigen . Healthcare should be accessible without forcing patients, physicians, and staff to carry the weight of a broken system. Tonight, I used Praxigen to write my mom's appeal letter. Now we wait... and keep on building for the millions more who are facing it too. #PriorAuthorization #HealthTech #PatientAdvocacy #HealthcareInnovation #Praxigen 🩵 ...more ...more

I just finished my summer internship as a Product Manager at Microsoft , and I wanted to take a moment to reflect on what I learned over the last three months. I worked on the Word Copilot team, specifically focused on agent evaluations. While I had experience using agents, this internship enabled me to build and evaluate agents at scale. My biggest takeaway was how much evaluation infrastructure shapes the product itself. Working through user-intent classification, data drift, and designing evals that actually reflected real usage made it clear that whatever you choose to measure becomes what the team optimizes for. Evals are closer to a product spec than a quality gate. I also learned how much iteration goes into improving AI products. Running experiments and navigating tradeoffs between quality, latency, and cost reinforced the importance of pairing technical understanding with strong product judgment. Most importantly, customer obsession remained the guiding principle. With agents, it’s easy to chase better metrics or greater capability, but what matters is whether we’re ultimately driving better outcomes for customers. Grateful to Caroline Brown , Maritza Cartaya , and the many others who made these three months such a meaningful experience. I'm excited to take these lessons with me into my next chapter!

Been working on something with my dad the past few months that I really wish existed two years ago. Built from something painfully real: my own college process, and now my sister's too. Two years ago I was in the thick of college applications, and even with an expensive counselor, figuring out my actual chances anywhere felt like guesswork. My dad ended up spending days manually researching schools with me comparing programs, requirements, all of it. It's not until you're actually in the Common App selecting majors that you realize there are literally hundreds of them. We picked based on gut feel and interest because there was no way to know more than that. I got lucky and I got into USC, into the major I dreamed of, but "hope" isn't a strategy, and it definitely shouldn't have to be. If we'd had something that could tell us my odds per major at each school, not just a generic acceptance rate, and help build a real application strategy around that, we could've saved hours of research and thousands of dollars on counselors. That's why this matters to me. Applications just opened. If you know a student staring down this process right now, this could save them the exact stress I went through. 👉 stratiaadmissions.com

Turns out writing a graduation speech is the easy part. But writing one that's actually memorable, and doesn't sound like it was written by ChatGPT at 2am (those who saw me writing the last paragraph with a pen and paper from the pocket of my dress the day of grad can attest that it wasn't), is significantly harder. Earlier this summer, I had the honor of delivering the graduation speech for Dougherty Valley High School's Class of 2026. I thought harder than I expected to about what's actually worth saying to a room full of people about to scatter in a hundred different directions. The main message I decided on was this: we carry immensely more influence on the world around us than we think, and we shape our reality by the perspectives we choose to hold on to and let go of. Everything I said that day, I owe to the people who taught, encouraged, and enabled me to say it. Thank you to my teachers, mentors, coaches, family, and friends who supported me long before there was a podium involved. Finally thank you to my classmates, who made the last four years worth writing about in the first place. Excited to see what happens next!

Hot take: a blockchain-based fintech just had nearly a million customer records stolen. They had a $3.2B valuation. They presumably had audits. They presumably had certifications. Figure, the San Francisco-based lending platform, disclosed earlier this year that hackers made off with personal information on close to one million customers: names, addresses, dates of birth, phone numbers, and email addresses. The company was quick to note that Social Security numbers and financial account details weren't part of it. Which is true. And also a little beside the point. Here's what actually stood out to me: cybersecurity researchers linked the attack to ShinyHunters, a group that's been responsible for some of the largest breaches of the last few years. This wasn't a novel, unpredictable threat. It was a known actor using known methods against a company that, by all appearances, was doing things right. That's the part worth sitting with. Not "how did they get breached" but "what did their risk posture actually look like the day before this happened?" Did their compliance program reflect that exposure? Did anyone own that question? Regulators have been ramping up scrutiny of security practices at digital-first financial companies, and the CFPB has made clear that fintech firms face the same data protection obligations as traditional banks. The enforcement pressure is real. But enforcement pressure drives documentation. It doesn't automatically drive the kind of continuous, operational risk awareness that would have flagged this earlier. This is exactly the pattern I've been researching. 🔍 Most companies don't lose control of their risk management on purpose. It happens gradually, usually right around the time they start scaling. I've been digging into this lately: how security and compliance functions evolve as companies grow, particularly around frameworks like SOC 2 and ISO 27001. What's interesting isn't the frameworks themselves, it's what happens to risk management once those frameworks enter the picture. In the early days, risk feels intuitive. A small team knows where the soft spots are because they built the thing. But as companies scale and compliance requirements show up, often driven by a customer deal or an investor requirement, something subtle shifts. Risk management starts getting defined by what the audit checks for, rather than the audit reflecting what the company is actually worried about. The checklist becomes the risk model. That's not a criticism of the frameworks. It's a pretty natural response to growth; you need something standardized once you can't rely on tribal knowledge anymore. But people I've talked with described a real moment of realization: passing an audit and still not feeling like they had a handle on their actual exposure. The certification and the confidence stopped moving together. I'm still working through what makes the difference. The AI infrastructure buildout is one of the fastest capital deployment cycles in history. The security programs around it are not keeping up. In 2025 alone, U.S. data center construction starts reached $77.7 billion; a 190% year-over-year increase. In the first half of 2026, another $88 billion in projects are set to break ground. Hyperscalers are moving at a pace the security industry hasn't had to match before. AI data centers are being built faster than they can be secured. And the security challenge isn't just scale, it's structural. These aren't traditional data centers running independent servers. 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐲'𝐫𝐞 𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐥𝐞, 𝐦𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐧𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐞𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬 where a vulnerability in one layer: firmware, network interconnects, multi-tenant isolation, can cascade in ways that a standard risk framework wasn't designed to model. The pattern is familiar. A new capability gets deployed at speed. The risk program tries to catch up. 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐠𝐚𝐩 𝐛𝐞𝐭𝐰𝐞𝐞𝐧 𝐝𝐞𝐩𝐥𝐨𝐲𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐭𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐢𝐬 𝐰𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐥𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐬, and in most organizations, that gap is neither measured nor reported. Speed is a competitive advantage until it isn't. The compliance programs that were built for last decade's infrastructure aren't automatically equipped for this one. #Cybersecurity #AIInfrastructure #RiskManagement #DataCenterSecurity #SecurityPosture #Research

A number came out last week that I haven't been able to stop thinking about. Orca Security's 2026 State of AI Security Report, which pulled telemetry from over 1,200 production cloud environments, found that 99.9% of AI vulnerability alerts with an available fix remain unpatched. 81.2% of companies running AI packages have at least one known vulnerability. These aren't theoretical exposures or edge cases. These are known issues, with fixes available, sitting unaddressed across the majority of organizations that have deployed AI into production. The reason isn't negligence. It's prioritization, and 𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐳𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐢𝐬 𝐝𝐨𝐰𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐦 𝐨𝐟 𝐡𝐨𝐰 𝐲𝐨𝐮 𝐦𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐤. If your compliance program tells you you're secure because your controls are documented and your last audit was clean, there's no built-in signal telling you to go patch the AI package your engineering team quietly spun up six months ago. 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐚𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐭 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐬𝐤 𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐭 𝐰𝐚𝐬𝐧'𝐭 𝐝𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐤 𝐟𝐨𝐫. Organizations are building, deploying, and operating AI in the cloud, but basic cybersecurity hygiene is often being sacrificed for speed. That tradeoff might feel invisible right now. It tends to become very visible very quickly. This is the gap between certified and actually protected, playing out at scale, in real time. #Cybersecurity #AIRisk #RiskManagement #SecurityCompliance #AIGovernance #Research

I was initially rejected from Y Combinator startup school. Found out I was accepted on Monday. To preface, The bay area last year more than changed my life, and I really regretted missing the application for yc sus 2025, so I was looking forward to sus 2026. To reconnecting with some friends and welcoming the incoming batch of new builders to the bay. So to say the rejection didn’t bother me would be an understatement. It stung — just not quite as deeply as it once would have. You might think you are doing everything right: Early startup experience both large and personal. Top cs degrees. A great operator network. An unwavering fire to keep showing up. Keep working. To create something meaningful. And still, the outcome may be a bit silly 🤪 Common life lesson that still never feels easy: effort does not guarantee recognition, and talent does not make us immune to rejection. So passion has to become the reason. When you care deeply enough about the work, the doors that open and close begin to matter less. Don’t get me wrong rejections still hurt, but you keep building because you cannot imagine doing anything else. You follow the path because it feels true to you, even when no one is watching and nothing is promised — expectations and reality become secondary. Celebrate when the door opens. Keep moving when it does not. Do not wait for the world to validate what already makes you feel alive. You are the author of your own life. And all your rejections and setbacks will start to sting a bit less.

Last month, we took on 6 new clients. The past couple weeks we've taken zero. Here's what's top of mind in Month 2 of Sapience : 1. Selling can be a drug - know when to stop As we started to get revenue momentum, there's been pull to stack more. But after closing a few deals, we quickly realized our ops could be more polished. So, we halted sales to prioritize customer experience. 2. Prioritize love of the game over short-term cash My 30 minute morning slots can either be sales calls or reading new research on seo/aeo. For any long term game, the latter is more important. 3. Don't let last week's priorities dictate today's actions. In any early-stage business/startup, the constraint changes every week. Two weeks ago, my inner dialogue was “how do we get customers," now it's "how can we attribute revenue at close certainty” 4. Don't hide behind vanity metrics Especially in seo/aeo, it's easy to point to "impressions" and "clicks" making an impact. In reality, conversions & attributable ROI are what create long term value - how do we prioritize the latter. More exciting updates coming soon

publications.title: 3D Lidar-Based Object Conditions in Adverse Weather Conditions
publications.subtitle: National High School Journal of Science
publications.description: This research focuses on the critical task of lidar-based 3D object detection for autonomous driving, specifically evaluating the performance of convolutional neural networks under adverse weather conditions. The paper examines two leading models, PointPillar and SECOND, both trained on the KITTI dataset in clear weather. Initially, these models achieved average precision values of 51.86% and 70.02%, respectively, under standard conditions. However, when tested on the Canadian Adverse Driving Dataset (CADC) with snowfall, their precision dropped to nearly 0%, highlighting the challenge of object detection in real-world weather conditions. Retraining the models on CADC improved their precision to 48.43% and 49.51%, but resulted in a 0% precision on the KITTI dataset. This study stresses the importance of retraining models for specific environmental conditions to ensure reliable performance in autonomous driving applications.

Demis Hassabis told a room full of YC founders that agents are missing something fundamental. His take: agents today are fire and forget. They can't adapt to the specific context you put them in. They don't learn from the environment they're operating in. And until that's solved, they won't reach their full potential. He hasn't seen the breakout result yet either. No AAA game built by agents topping the charts. No kid shipping a 10 million copy hit. Something is still missing in the process or the tools. That part stuck with me because it's exactly what we see at Moda (YC W26) every day. Agents don't fail because the models are bad. They fail because they don't understand the context they're dropped into. The models are getting smarter. But smart without context is just expensive guessing. We're still in the experimentation phase. Demis said it, and I believe it. The real agent era hasn't started yet. ...more

Imagine accidentally committing an API key… Yeah. That sinking feeling when a secret you were supposed to protect is exposed… it can cost hours, millions, or even your reputation. And it happens to everyone, even the most experienced developers. And the scale of this problem is staggering: in 2023 alone, 12.8 million secrets were leaked on public GitHub repos. And less than 20 days ago, 3,325 secrets were compromised in the Ghost Action supply chain attack affecting PyPI, npm, and DockerHub tokens. That’s why Ritwic Verma and I took on the challenge of building ripenv last weekend at HackGT 12, submitting it to the Warp Best Dev Tool Challenge. ripenv is a secure environment manager built to make accidental leaks nearly impossible. .env files are encrypted client-side, keys are wrapped per teammate, and nothing ever leaves your machine in plaintext. ripenv includes both a CLI powered by Google Gemini for natural language management of secrets, and a web interface made using Next.js and Supabase for project-level secret management and teammate collaboration. No secrets touch our servers. No central vault to compromise. No blind trust in a third party. We don’t - and can’t - see your API keys. And if you’d rather keep everything in-house, ripenv can be deployed internally with the same guarantees. The result? Teams can commit .env files to GitHub, share them across teammates, and push them through CI/CD pipelines - without ever exposing a single secret. Even if the file goes public, it’s just ciphertext. With ripenv, leaking secrets is no longer a risk. Overall, HackGT 12 was an amazing experience. We got to meet incredible people from Warp , Ergo , Visa , and many other companies. A special thanks to Advait Maybhate and Varoon Kodithala for their guidance and invaluable feedback. Huge thanks also to HexLabs, Inc. for hosting the event! No more sending out your API keys over Discord. This past weekend at Hack GT 12, Himansh Chitkara and I built ripenv, a comprehensive solution for managing secrets across development teams. The software industry is facing a growing secrets management crisis. Millions of API keys, tokens, and credentials get exposed every year through public repos, messy pipelines, or supply chain breaches ( https://lnkd.in/gWTPGmb4 ) . We wanted to build something that helps developers and organizations avoid those catastrophic leaks. The idea wasn’t just to lock secrets away, but to do it with a zero-trust, security-first approach while still keeping things simple and smooth for developers. We built a dashboard with Next.js and Supabase for managing team permissions, and a developer-first CLI that understands natural language thanks to Google Gemini. With CI/CD integration for automated secret rotations and a zero-knowledge design, ripenv protects your secrets as seamlessly as Git manages your code. I had the chance to meet some amazing people at HackGT 12, including folks from Warp , Cedar , and several other companies. A picture is worth a thousand words? More like, a solid portfolio is worth a thousand resumes (you get the point 🤪) This is how I’m building my portfolio before recruiting is in full swing, and how you can build yours too :) Yesterday, I told you about requirements: that helped me nail the content for my portfolio. I want to talk about the design part today, 𝘀𝗼 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝘁𝗿𝘆 𝗶𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳 𝗯𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗙𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝟱 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝘂𝘀𝗮𝗴𝗲-𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝟭𝟵𝘁𝗵. I saw a video where Nick Saraev generated 25 website designs with Fable and was genuinely blown away (!) So I tried it out with building my portfolio and generated 25 design directions in one afternoon. I put two constraints on Fable first: 𝗦𝗲𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁. This is the mistake I actually made the first time: I gave Fable everything I had written about my projects and asked it for 25 directions. But because I was trying to solve two problems at once, I was basically getting mush (and blowing through *way* more tokens than I’d like to admit). When I ran it again, this time with just design + only the titles of my projects, it finally worked :) 𝗗𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗹𝗮𝘆𝗼𝘂𝘁𝘀 𝘁𝗼𝗼, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝘆𝗹𝗲. I learned that I like seeing all my projects in one glance. But you might like a carousel structure, which goes through your projects one by one. We’re not going to know until we’ve seen both. 𝗕𝗮𝘀𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗧𝗟𝗗𝗥: I think you’ve got pretty good taste. You’ll see something and know immediately if you like it or not. But it’s way harder to imagine your way to what you like, and you definitely can’t give feedback on something that doesn’t exist yet. Portfolio Spotlight: Hex Security (YC W26) Most companies still rely on periodic penetration testing. But software now ships continuously, and the gap between audits is often where vulnerabilities emerge. In mid-September 2025, Anthropic detected a Chinese state-sponsored cyber-espionage campaign that used AI to automate 80 to 90% of attack activity, with the system making thousands of requests, often multiple per second. "oMg ur fRoM gUaM???" Roughly 738,383 times I've heard this, between my first year at Stanford and my months in SF. I don't mind, though. It's kind of nice being the first person from Guam someone's ever met. 🇬🇺 But here's what I never get to say in those thirty-second conversations: Guam is where I transformed myself, quite literally and figuratively. I moved to Guam right at the start of 6th grade, and some of my classmates would ask where I was from and whether I could even speak English. I was overweight, not confident, and reserved until the pandemic. Maybe it's because Guam is so influenced by the military, I don't know, but my routine during COVID became as disciplined as an actual military schedule: wake up, eat, read books, study vocab, go out and work out for two to three hours, come back for family discussion, and sleep — on repeat. Actually keeping my promises to myself gifted me confidence. Soon after, I entered 9th grade and followed my older sister into JROTC. This essentially became the core of my high school experience. From staying back after school to train for fitness competitions, to standing for long hours in our perfectly ironed uniforms under the sun for ceremonies, to handing out letters to veterans on Veterans Day, to the countless hours we spent preparing for Army inspection. Gosh, this program truly shaped me. Beneath all of these events were the discipline, the teamwork, and the commitment. Looking back, I had the Army LDRSHIP values memorized in the back of my head throughout high school. Now, trying to write them out a year later, I can only remember half of them — but instead of cheating myself, I'll type out exactly what I remember: Loyalty, Respect, Selfless Service, Honor, Integrity, Personal Courage... just can't remember D, I guess lol. What I do remember, though, is how deeply one thing was ingrained in me: one drop of water is powerless, but together we are an ocean. Leading 200 cadets as Executive Officer by junior year, I truly learned how important it is to have everyone aligned on the same VISION and to lead by example. It was never "I'll check up on them when it's convenient." It was always "I'll help you from the very first step." And that is exactly why I am so obsessed with community building and human effort. Because I have SEEN with my own two eyes how a shy, reserved girl went on to become battalion commander four years later. Because I have SEEN how a guy I met freshman year, who was going through the hardest stretch of his life, later told me I inspired him to set goals and work toward them. He went on to join the Air Force. The years of effort, the days we doubted ourselves, the days we made breakthroughs, the endless emotions we overcame — THAT is exactly what AI cannot fake. And that is exactly why I am creating a passport of human effort @ commit.social . The website is live. Come leave your first proof of effort. 🌊

ADUs Are One of California's Most Successful Housing Programs. San José homeowners filed 1,806 ADU applications across 2023–2025 - 50 a month, on average, for 36 straight months. Through the hardest capital-markets stretch of this development cycle, while approved multifamily projects sat waiting at the financing gate, the ADU application curve didn't move. The geography is 29 ZIP codes, with the five busiest hold just 22% of the volume. This is parcel-by-parcel production across all single-family zoning districts citywide. The full breakdown of why the math works is now at https://lnkd.in/gTkRP7qj : → The two rulebooks: San José's City track (up to 1,200 sf) vs. the State track (800 sf, exempt from lot coverage and FAR) - the same parcel can pencil under one and fail under the other. → The 750 sq ft impact fee requirements: SB 543 made the impact-fee exemption inclusive (≤750 sf of interior livable space) as of January 2026. → California's first standalone ADU sale closed in June: $530K for a 749 sf two-bedroom near downtown, through the AB 1033 condo pathway San José adopted first. Plus two tools: a map of all geocoded applications, and a quick-screen calculator that runs track eligibility, fee flags, and gross yield on your numbers.

Seattle published a library of pre-approved ADU designs. Permitting doubled. Here's how it works: the city pre-clears ADU plans that already meet code, pass structural review, and include engineering. A homeowner picks a design off the shelf and skips the plan-check queue. The Pew Charitable Trusts studied 40 cities running similar programs. Results: - Permitting timelines drop by months - Construction costs fall $5,000-$10,000 per unit - Homeowners and small builders can actually participate Permitting costs and timelines are where ADU production stalls. Pre-approved plans remove that friction at the source. The cheapest housing policy any city can run.

projects.description: SnapCycle is a mobile app built with Expo and React Native on the front end and Python with FastAPI on the back end. A user snaps a photo of an item, and Google Gemini Vision Model names it. The app then runs the item through a chain of small AI agents that check a Redis backed knowledge base built per zip code and use Browserbase to read real local web pages. This lets the app point the user to a true fix, such as a home bin, a gift drop off, a city bulk pickup, or a junk haul firm. When a haul firm is the right path, the backend uses Twilio to text all local firms at once and stream their price quotes back live. projects.title: SpeakEase
projects.description: SpeakEase marked a meaningful step in addressing language barriers through personalized, AI-powered learning. Developed to support non-native English speakers, SpeakEase offers an interactive and conversational platform that adapts to the user's language level, helping them practice English in real-world contexts while building confidence through dialogue and quizzes.In collaboration with a developer peer, we built the platform’s backend and AI integration. I focused on implementing the AI components, using a customized wrapper to create a chatbot capable of natural language interaction. This system dynamically adjusted its responses based on user input, offering tailored language support and improving engagement. My partner developed the user authentication system and frontend UI using Mongoose and React, enabling smooth onboarding and an intuitive user experience.To further personalize the learning process, we added a quiz-generation feature that creates practice questions based on each user's conversational history. This reinforced key vocabulary and grammar structures, providing a complete learning loop. The system was designed to scale, with architecture ready to support multilingual features in future iterations.SpeakEase showcased the power of AI in education, bridging communication gaps while blending machine learning with human-centered design. It stands as a testament to how accessible, thoughtful technology can drive meaningful impact for language learners around the world.

projects.title: Monify
projects.description: Monify marked my first major initiative aimed at enhancing financial literacy among high school students. Designed as a comprehensive budgeting tool, it empowers students to track their spending, set financial goals, and manage their budgets with an intuitive and user-friendly interface.For backend development, I utilized Flask and PyCharm, leveraging Flask-SQLAlchemy with PostgreSQL to ensure secure and efficient data management. This implementation allowed users to store, retrieve, and modify financial data seamlessly, providing a structured and reliable system for expense tracking. During testing phases, an isolated PostgreSQL instance was employed to evaluate database performance, optimize queries, and enhance overall system efficiency.On the frontend, I incorporated Tailwind CSS to create a modern, responsive UI, ensuring an accessible and visually appealing experience across various devices. The design prioritized ease of use, allowing students to quickly input, analyze, and adjust their financial habits.Monify gained traction within the Pleasanton Unified School District, with over 50 students participating in the initial testing phase. This project not only reinforced the importance of financial education in high schools but also demonstrated the potential of technology-driven solutions in fostering responsible financial habits among students.For more details and additional projects, visit my portfolio.

projects.title: PrimeStats
projects.description: PrimeStats was designed as a centralized sports platform for Cross Country and Track athletes, providing a real-time feed of sports news, healthy recipes, and personal goal tracking. Developed using React and Visual Studio Code, the platform served as a daily resource for student-athletes looking to stay informed, improve their nutrition, and set personal fitness goals.To keep the project small-scale and efficient, I integrated Google Firebase for lightweight data storage and user authentication, ensuring a seamless experience for athletes to track their personal notes and progress. Additionally, I incorporated local APIs to provide daily healthy recipes, offering nutritional recommendations tailored for endurance athletes.The platform gained popularity within the Pleasanton Unified School District, supporting student-athletes throughout a full Cross Country and Track season. However, due to financial limitations in securing a dedicated domain and database hosting, the project was eventually phased out. Despite this, PrimeStats demonstrated the value of accessible, digital resources for student-athletes, reinforcing the potential of technology in promoting sports engagement and wellness.For more details on my work, visit my portfolio.
